<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-framed cases and the clash narrowed usefully. PRO's core move — licensing inverts who bears the cost of uncertainty, so unresolved questions default to "not yet" — was genuinely strong, and its tu quoque (the AI Act's systemic-risk chapter rests on the same unverifiable self-assessments, with no gate and no revocation) put real pressure on CON. But CON handled that pressure more cleanly than PRO handled CON's. CON's answer to PRO's Q1 was honest and reframing rather than evasive: it conceded "none," then showed the regimes operate at different layers, with risk-based biting where harms announce themselves and licensing making the one undetectable claim (capability evaluation) the load-bearing wall. That answer converted PRO's best attack into a comparison CON preferred. CON also mined PRO's own concessions effectively — that licensing is "additive," and that day-one thresholds would be codified from frameworks "the labs themselves already publish," which CON turned into industry-calibrated gatekeeping plus regulatory capture. Meanwhile several CON burdens stayed thin for PRO: entrenchment of incumbents got only opening-level assertion, and extraterritorial evasion ("a lab denied in Brussels releases from elsewhere; only European open developers are shut out") drew just a one-line appeal to single-market leverage in closing. PRO retained real unique offense in the irreversible open-release case with no downstream deployer, but CON blunted it twice (existing pre-deployment GPAI duties; refusal cannot recall weights). PRO also absorbed two clipped turns to CON's one, costing it weighing space at exactly the moments it needed to close those gaps. Rhetorically the two were near-equal ("Ask first, or find out later" vs "Asking is not a safety technique. Knowing is."), so the edge falls to the side whose objections survived: CON.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 2 answer to PRO's Q1: rather than dodging, CON conceded "none," then argued the regimes don't compete at that layer — risk-based catches observable, provable downstream harms, while licensing elevates an unverifiable capability representation into a certificate that teaches deployers to stop checking. Combined with the extracted concession that PRO's own day-one thresholds would be borrowed from industry-published frameworks, this reframed PRO's strongest attack into CON's false-assurance case.</best_rebuttal>
